Fit a growth curve

Source: R/gcTMB.R
gcTMB.Rd

Fits a nonlinear growth curve over time by maximum likelihood with the Template Model Builder (TMB), optionally with covariates on the parameters and random effects, which are integrated out by the Laplace approximation.

Usage

gcTMB(
  form,
  fform = NULL,
  rform = NULL,
  data,
  start = NULL,
  fix = NULL,
  correlation = NULL,
  variance = NULL,
  lower = -Inf,
  upper = Inf,
  family = "gaussian",
  model = "logistic",
  truncated = TRUE,
  link = NULL,
  b1type = c("asymptote", "rate"),
  weights = NULL,
  gsl = NULL,
  gsu = NULL,
  gsn = NULL,
  control = list()
)

Arguments

form

Formula, with the names of the response and the explanatory variable x, e.g. weight ~ day. x is usually time, but can be any variable along which the response grows towards an asymptote, e.g. the diameter of trees in a height-diameter model height ~ dbh.

fform

Formula, list of formulas, or NULL. Fixed effects for the model parameters: a formula of the form b1 + b2 ~ Treatment, or a list of such formulas, e.g. list(b1 ~ Treatment, b2 ~ Treatment + Site). Parameters not listed have a single intercept (~ 1); NULL (default) gives every parameter a single intercept, one curve for all the data. A list of five right-hand side formulas, one for each of b1-b5 (X1 = ~ 1, ..., X5 = ~ 1), is also accepted.

rform

Formula, list of formulas, or NULL. Random effects: a formula of the form b1 + b2 ~ 1 | ID for random intercepts, or b1 ~ x | ID for random intercepts and slopes in a covariate x, or a list of such formulas, e.g. list(b1 + b2 ~ 1 | ID, b1 ~ 1 | site). The random effects within a formula are correlated across the listed parameters and their intercepts and slopes; different formulas and the levels of nested factors (1 | site/ID) are independent terms. With a double bar, all the random coefficients of the formula are independent, across the parameters as well as their intercepts and slopes: b1 + b2 ~ 1 || ID is list(b1 ~ 1 | ID, b2 ~ 1 | ID), a diagonal covariance matrix as random=pdDiag(b1 + b2 ~ 1) in nlme. A list of formulas combines the two into a block-diagonal covariance matrix: list(b1 + b2 ~ 1 | ID, b3 ~ 1 | ID) gives correlated random effects of b1 and b2, and a random effect of b3 independent of both, as random=pdBlocked(list(pdSymm(b1 + b2 ~ 1), pdSymm(b3 ~ 1))) in nlme. The random slopes of a parameter usually go with a fixed effect of the covariate in fform. NULL (default) for no random effects.

data

Data frame. Observations with missing values in the variables of the model or in the weights are left out.

start

Numeric vector or NULL. Starting values for each model coefficient. NA entries are replaced by the starting values of gcTMBstart, and NULL (default) uses them for all coefficients. Alternatively, a vector named by parameter, e.g. c(b1=10), gives the same starting value to all coefficients of each named parameter.

fix

Logical vector or NULL. One entry for each model coefficient. If TRUE, a model coefficient is fixed to its value in start. Alternatively, a vector named by parameter, e.g. c(b1=TRUE), fixes all coefficients of the named parameters; their values must then be given in start, e.g. start=c(b1=10). NULL (default) fixes only the parameters that are fixed by default. The threshold (start of growth) b4 and the asymmetry b5 are fixed by default, at b4 = 0 (the curve starts at zero at t = 0) and b5 = 1 (the symmetric curve) unless given in start; so is the intercept b4 of the chapmanrichards and korf models, at the breast height of 1.3, while the rates b4 and b5 of the preecebaines model are estimated; fix=c(b4=FALSE) or fix=c(b5=FALSE), or an unnamed fix vector, estimates them. Without truncation, b4 is not used and always fixed, at 0 unless given in start.

correlation

A correlation structure or NULL. The autocorrelation of the residuals within groups over time, corAR1, corCAR1, corExp or corGaus (or the same structures of the package nlme), e.g. corCAR1(form=~ time | ID), for the gaussian and lognormal (on the log scale) families. NULL (default) for independent residuals. See corStruct; with a correlation structure, the weights are precision weights, with residual variance sigma^2/w.

variance

A variance function or NULL. Heteroscedastic residuals with the standard deviation sigma g, varIdent, varPower or varConstPower (or the same functions of the package nlme), e.g. varIdent(form=~ 1 | Treatment) for a variance for each treatment, or varConstPower(form=~ rate(.)) for a standard deviation that grows with the growth rate of the curve, for the gaussian and lognormal (on the log scale) families. NULL (default) for a constant variance. See varFunc.

lower

Numeric, a single value or a vector. Lower bounds for the model coefficients b1-b5, a single value or a vector with the same length as start. Bounds of fixed coefficients are ignored; variance parameters are unbounded.

upper

Numeric, a single value or a vector. Upper bounds for the model coefficients b1-b5, a single value or a vector with the same length as start.

family

Character string. The distribution of the response, one of "gaussian", "lognormal", "binomial", "betabinomial", "beta", "poisson", "nbinom2", and "nbinom1". For the lognormal family, log(y) is normal with mean log f(t) and standard deviation sigma: the curve f is the median of a positive response, with a constant coefficient of variation; the mean is f(t) exp(sigma^2/2). The negative binomial families are for overdispersed counts, with variance mu (1 + mu/theta) for nbinom2 and mu (1 + phi) for nbinom1, and the beta-binomial family for overdispersed binomial counts, with variance n mu (1 - mu) (1 + (n - 1)/(phi + 1)) for n trials, as in glmmTMB.

model

Character string. The growth model: "logistic" (default), "gompertz", "hill", "weibull", "normal" or "gamma", each with an asymmetry parameter b5, "beta" or "beta_capped" for determinate growth, "chapmanrichards" or "korf" for height-diameter models in forestry, "preecebaines" for human growth in height, or "linear" for a straight line, see Details.

truncated

Logical. If TRUE (default), the curve is truncated at a threshold time b4, by default fixed at 0: the response is zero up to b4 and then grows, see Details. FALSE for the curves without truncation. The beta, beta_capped, chapmanrichards, korf and preecebaines curves are never truncated.

link

Named character vector or NULL. Links of the parameters b1-b5: NULL for the defaults, or links named by parameter, e.g. link=c(b1="log", b3="inverse"). The default is the identity link for all parameters, except the shape b3 of the weibull, gamma and korf models, which must be larger than 1 and has the link "logm1", log(b3 - 1), by default (link=c(b3="identity") gives the shape itself). The links available for each parameter depend on its role in the model:

  • the asymptote b1: "identity", "log" or "logit" (for proportions); the slope b1 of the linear model: "identity" or "log";

  • the time b2 (inflection point, half the asymptote, middle of puberty), the rate b2 of chapmanrichards and the coefficient b2 of korf: "identity" or "log"; the intercept b2 of the linear model: "identity";

  • a scale b3 (logistic, gompertz, normal): "identity", "inverse", with which its coefficients are the growth rate 1/b3, or "log"; the shape b3 of weibull, gamma and korf: "logm1", "identity" or "log"; any other b3 (the slope of hill, the shape of chapmanrichards, the end of growth of beta, the height of preecebaines): "identity" or "log";

  • b4 (the threshold or start of growth, the intercept of chapmanrichards and korf, the rate of preecebaines) and the asymmetry b5: "identity" or "log".

A link that a model does not allow gives an error naming the allowed ones. The coefficients, and start, fix, lower, upper and curves of timeto, are on the scale of the links, see Details.

b1type

Character string. The meaning of b1: "asymptote" (default), or "rate" for the maximum growth rate of the curve, see Details. With "rate", covariates and random effects on b1 are effects on the maximum growth rate, which anova.gcTMB and partest can test.

weights

Numeric vector or NULL. Weights, one for each row of data; NULL (default) for a weight of 1 for every row. Unlike the weights of nlme, which are variance functions (varFunc), these are numeric case weights of the log-likelihood; with a correlation structure, they are precision weights, as weights=varFixed(~ 1/w) in nlme.

gsl

Numeric vector or NULL. Lower bounds for a grid search, same length as start; NA for the default range. If gsl, gsu and gsn are all NULL (default), no grid search is performed and the starting values come from linear models (method "lm" of gcTMBstart); if any of them is given, NULL for the others means the default ranges and 10 grid points. See gcTMBstart.

gsu

Numeric vector or NULL. Upper bounds for a grid search, same length as start; NA for the default range, see gsl for NULL.

gsn

Integer, a single number or a vector, or NULL. Number of grid points for each parameter, a single number or a vector with the same length as start. gsn=10 alone runs a grid search over the default ranges; see gsl for NULL.

control

List. Control parameters, the arguments of gcTMBcontrol, e.g. list(iter.max=2000). See gcTMBcontrol for details.

Value

A gcTMB object, with methods for print, summary, coef, vcov, predict, confint, anova, plot and others, see gcTMB-methods.

Details

The logistic, gompertz, hill, weibull, normal and gamma curves are sigmoid growth curves, often used in agronomy and ecology; they increase from 0 towards the asymptote b1:

  • logistic: f(t) = b1 / (1 + exp(-(t - b2)/b3)), symmetric around b2, where the curve reaches half of its asymptote;

  • gompertz: f(t) = b1 exp(-exp(-(t - b2)/b3)); it reaches exp(-1), about 37\ asymptote at b2 and approaches the asymptote more slowly than it leaves zero;

  • hill: f(t) = b1 / (1 + (b2/t)^b3), a logistic curve in log t (log-logistic), b1 / (1 + exp(-b3 (log t - log b2))); b2 is the time at which the curve reaches half of its asymptote, and b3 the slope on the log time axis;

  • weibull: f(t) = b1 (1 - exp(-(b3 - 1)/b3 (t/b2)^b3)); b2 is the inflection point and b3 > 1 the shape;

  • normal: f(t) = b1 Phi((t - b2)/b3), with the standard normal distribution function Phi; symmetric around b2, where the curve reaches half of its asymptote;

  • gamma: f(t) = b1 F(t), with F the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the gamma distribution with shape b3 > 1 and scale b2/(b3 - 1), whose density has its mode at b2: b2 is the inflection point and b3 the shape;

  • linear: f(t) = b1 t + b2, a straight line with slope b1 and intercept b2, for comparison with the growth curves. It has no asymptote, does not use b3-b5 and is not truncated; timeto gives the times at which it reaches given responses (type="absolute"), and maxrate its constant rate b1.

Five more curves are never truncated: the beta curves of determinate growth, the height-diameter models chapmanrichards and korf, common in forestry, and the preecebaines model of human growth:

  • chapmanrichards: f(t) = b4 + b1 (1 - exp(-b2 t))^b3, the Chapman-Richards curve of Richards (1959) in its usual form for height-diameter models, zero above the intercept b4 up to t = 0: b1 is the asymptote, b2 the rate, b3 the shape and b4 the intercept, fixed by default at the breast height of 1.3 m (start=c(b4=0) for a curve from zero, fix=c(b4=FALSE) to estimate it). For b3 > 1 the inflection point is at log(b3)/b2, where the curve reaches (1 - 1/b3)^b3 of its asymptote; for b3 <= 1 it grows fastest at t = 0;

  • beta: the beta growth function of Yin et al. (2003), eqn 8 (with b4 = 0 there), f(t) = b1 (1 + (b3 - t)/(b3 - b2)) ((t - b4)/(b3 - b4))^((b3 - b4)/(b3 - b2)) for b4 < t < 2 b3 - b2, and zero otherwise: b1 is the maximum w_max, b2 the time t_m of the maximum growth rate, b3 the end of growth t_e, where the curve reaches b1, and b4 the start of growth t_b, b4 < b2 < b3. After b3 the curve falls back to zero at 2 b3 - b2, for responses that decline after their maximum, e.g. biomass lost after maturity;

  • beta_capped: the same curve up to b3, and b1 from b3 on, the beta sigmoid growth function of Yin et al. for determinate growth that stops at its maximum;

  • korf: f(t) = b4 + b1 exp(b2/((1 - b3) t^(b3 - 1))) for t > 0, and b4 up to t = 0, the Korf curve: b1 is the asymptote above the intercept b4, b2 > 0 a coefficient, b3 > 1 the shape, and b4 the intercept as for chapmanrichards. The inflection point is at t = (b2/b3)^(1/(b3 - 1)), where the curve reaches exp(-b3/(b3 - 1)) of its asymptote;

  • preecebaines: model 1 of Preece and Baines (1978) for human growth in height, f(t) = b1 - 2 (b1 - b3)/(exp(b4 (t - b2)) + exp(b5 (t - b2))): the adult height b1, the age b2 in the middle of puberty, the height b3 at b2, and the rates b4 < b5 of growth before and during puberty, which are estimated by default. maxrate gives the peak of the pubertal growth spurt (the peak height velocity); b1type="rate" is not available.

Relation to nlme. Parts of the interface follow the package nlme (Pinheiro and Bates, 2000), so that models can be moved between nlme::nlme/nlme::gnls and gcTMB:

  • the fixed and random effects are formulas for the parameters, as the arguments fixed and random of nlme::nlme: fform=b1 + b2 ~ trt or fform=list(b1 ~ trt, b2 ~ 1), and rform=b1 + b2 ~ 1 | ID. The random effects of a formula have an unstructured covariance matrix, as pdSymm; uncorrelated random effects, as pdDiag, are separate terms, e.g. rform=list(b1 ~ 1 | ID, b2 ~ 1 | ID) or b1 ~ x || ID. Nested factors (1 | site/ID) and the double bar use the syntax of lme4;

  • the correlation structures corAR1, corCAR1, corExp and corGaus have the arguments and the parameterisation of nlme, whose objects are accepted as well, and residuals(fit, type="normalized") gives the normalized residuals of nlme;

  • the variance functions varIdent, varPower and varConstPower go in the argument variance (the argument weights of nlme), with the arguments and parameterisation of nlme, plus the growth rate rate(.) as a covariate;

  • fixef, ranef and VarCorr are generics with the names of those of nlme, and work for gcTMB, nlme and lme4 fits whichever package is attached last;

  • predict and fitted with random=FALSE correspond to level=0 of nlme (the population curves), and with random=TRUE to the innermost level.

The differences: gcTMB fits by maximum likelihood (the Laplace approximation with random effects), so its log-likelihoods, AIC and likelihood ratio tests compare with nlme fits with method="ML", not with the default REML of nlme::lme and nlme::gls; the integration over the random effects is exact for gaussian responses with random effects that enter the curve linearly, e.g. random asymptotes, where nlme's linearisation can stop slightly short of the maximum. coef returns the estimated coefficients and variance parameters, not the coefficients of each group as coef of nlme (use predict(fit, type="parameters") for those); weights are numeric weights, not variance functions; and the results of ranef and VarCorr have the format of lme4 (a list of data frames, and of covariance matrices). confint.gcTMB gives the intervals of intervals of nlme.

The asymmetry b5, the truncation at the threshold b4, the maximum growth rates and inflection points, the rate 1/b3 and the small-sample inference are described in the vignette, vignette("gcTMB"); the links in the argument link.

With b1type="rate", b1 is the maximum growth rate of the curve, the slope at its inflection point (see maxrate), instead of the asymptote; the asymptote is b1 divided by the maximum growth rate of the curve with asymptote 1, which depends on b2-b5. The model is the same as with the asymptote, unless b1 has random effects, which are then random maximum growth rates. predict(type="parameters") gives the asymptote as well. The maximum growth rate has a closed form for all the models with b5 = 1, and for the logistic (Richards) and hill curves also with an asymmetry b5; the gompertz, weibull, normal and gamma models need b5 fixed at 1. The hill curve has a maximum growth rate at a positive time only for b3 b5 > 1. For the linear model, b1 is the rate anyway.

References

Pinheiro, J.C. and Bates, D.M. (2000). Mixed-Effects Models in S and S-PLUS. Springer, New York.

Preece, M.A. and Baines, M.J. (1978). A new family of mathematical models describing the human growth curve. Annals of Human Biology 5, 1-24.

Richards, F.J. (1959). A flexible growth function for empirical use. Journal of Experimental Botany 10, 290-300.

Yin, X., Goudriaan, J., Lantinga, E.A., Vos, J. and Spiertz, H.J. (2003). A flexible sigmoid function of determinate growth. Annals of Botany 91, 361-371.

See also

maxrate for the maximum growth rate and its timing, timeto for the times to reach a level of the asymptote, gcTMBstart for the starting values.

Examples

# logistic growth of the faba bean plants
fit <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, model="logistic")
summary(fit)
#> Call:
#> gcTMB(form = Height ~ DAS, data = FabaHeights25, model = "logistic")
#> 
#> Model:  logistic, truncated at b4 = 0
#> Family: gaussian, identity link for all parameters
#> 
#> Number of observations: 200
#> Log-likelihood: -699.2 (df = 4), AIC: 1406, BIC: 1420
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> b1:(Intercept) 120.7851     3.6524   33.07   <2e-16 ***
#> b2:(Intercept)  30.7300     0.6822   45.05   <2e-16 ***
#> b3:(Intercept)  12.8808     0.9769   13.19   <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#> Residual standard deviation: 8.043 on 197 degrees of freedom
#> 
#> Optimiser: relative convergence (4), maximum absolute gradient 3.4e-08

# the other models, compared by AIC
fitg <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, model="gompertz")
fith <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, model="hill")
fitw <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, model="weibull")
fitn <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, model="normal")
fitgam <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, model="gamma")
fitlin <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, model="linear")
# the forestry models from zero instead of their default intercept, the breast height of 1.3 m
fitcr <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, model="chapmanrichards", start=c(b4=0))
fitb <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, model="beta_capped")
fitk <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, model="korf", start=c(b4=0))
AIC(fit, fitg, fith, fitw, fitn, fitgam, fitlin, fitcr, fitb, fitk)
#>        df      AIC
#> fit     4 1406.470
#> fitg    4 1407.658
#> fith    4 1409.892
#> fitw    4 1407.757
#> fitn    4 1406.412
#> fitgam  4 1409.685
#> fitlin  3 1443.592
#> fitcr   4 1410.100
#> fitb    4 1406.751
#> fitk    4 1415.341

# a height-diameter model from the breast height of 1.3 m, the default intercept b4
gcTMB(Height ~ DBH, data=PineHeightDiameter, model="chapmanrichards")
#> Call:
#> gcTMB(form = Height ~ DBH, data = PineHeightDiameter, model = "chapmanrichards")
#> 
#> Model:  chapmanrichards
#> Family: gaussian, identity link for all parameters
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> b1:(Intercept)  b2:(Intercept)  b3:(Intercept)  
#>       45.71868         0.01965         1.05978  
#> Fixed: b4:(Intercept) = 1.3
#> 
#> Residual standard deviation: 2.434

# the Richards curve: the logistic model with an estimated asymmetry b5
fitr5 <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, fix=c(b5=FALSE))
coef(fitr5)
#> b1:(Intercept) b2:(Intercept) b3:(Intercept) b5:(Intercept)      log_sigma 
#>    120.9525457     30.6657471     12.9844198      0.9728521      2.0772341 

# the rate 1/b3 instead of the scale b3
gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, link=c(b3="inverse"))
#> Call:
#> gcTMB(form = Height ~ DAS, data = FabaHeights25, link = c(b3 = "inverse"))
#> 
#> Model:  logistic, truncated at b4 = 0
#> Family: gaussian, inverse link for b3, identity link for the other parameters
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> b1:(Intercept)  b2:(Intercept)  b3:(Intercept)  
#>      120.78512        30.72998         0.07764  
#> 
#> Residual standard deviation: 8.043

# treatment effects on the asymptote as ratios, with the log link
FabaHeights25$trt <- factor(FabaHeights25$Treatment)
fitl <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, fform=b1 ~ trt, data=FabaHeights25, link=c(b1="log"))
exp(coef(fitl)[2:5])
#> b1:trt0.3 b1:trt0.5 b1:trt0.6 b1:trt0.8 
#>  1.007483  1.077149  1.075851  1.050422 

# treatment effects on the asymptote and random effects of the plants
FabaHeights25$trt <- factor(FabaHeights25$Treatment)
fitre <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, fform=b1 ~ trt, rform=b1 + b2 ~ 1 | Plant_ID, data=FabaHeights25)
summary(fitre)
#> Call:
#> gcTMB(form = Height ~ DAS, fform = b1 ~ trt, rform = b1 + b2 ~ 
#>     1 | Plant_ID, data = FabaHeights25)
#> 
#> Model:  logistic, truncated at b4 = 0
#> Family: gaussian, identity link for all parameters
#> 
#> Number of observations: 200, groups: Plant_ID 25
#> Log-likelihood: -509.5 (df = 11), AIC: 1041, BIC: 1077
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> b1:(Intercept) 115.7419     4.0576  28.525   <2e-16 ***
#> b1:trt0.3       -3.1569     5.6806  -0.556   0.5784    
#> b1:trt0.5        9.8502     5.5933   1.761   0.0782 .  
#> b1:trt0.6       11.1356     5.6175   1.982   0.0474 *  
#> b1:trt0.8        8.9832     5.6351   1.594   0.1109    
#> b2:(Intercept)  30.8745     0.5402  57.151   <2e-16 ***
#> b3:(Intercept)  12.8441     0.2498  51.418   <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> Unadjusted Wald tests; tests of the differences between curves adjusted for their number: partest().
#> 
#> Random effects:
#>  Groups   Name Std.Dev. Corr 
#>  Plant_ID b1   8.842         
#>           b2   2.550    -0.33
#> 
#> Residual standard deviation: 2.075
#> 
#> Optimiser: relative convergence (4), maximum absolute gradient 5.2e-05

# treatment effects on the maximum growth rate, b1 with b1type = "rate", tested by a likelihood
# ratio test and compared with the first treatment
fitr <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, fform=b1 + b2 ~ trt, data=FabaHeights25, b1type="rate")
fitr0 <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, fform=b2 ~ trt, data=FabaHeights25, b1type="rate")
anova(fitr0, fitr)
#> Likelihood ratio tests of gcTMB models
#> 
#>       npar    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance     LR Df  Pr(>LR)   
#> fitr0    8 1409.4 1435.8 -696.71   1393.4                      
#> fitr    12 1401.8 1441.4 -688.90   1377.8 15.619  4 0.003576 **
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
partest(fitr, newdata=data.frame(trt=levels(FabaHeights25$trt)))
#> Differences to the reference of b1 (maximum growth rate):
#> 
#>                   Estimate Std.Error t value p.value    lower upper
#> trt=0.3 - trt=0.1  -0.0149    0.0776  -0.193  0.9991 -0.20635 0.176
#> trt=0.5 - trt=0.1   0.2053    0.0822   2.498  0.0462  0.00247 0.408
#> trt=0.6 - trt=0.1   0.2180    0.0835   2.611  0.0344  0.01197 0.424
#> trt=0.8 - trt=0.1   0.1624    0.0839   1.937  0.1705 -0.04457 0.369
#> 
#> Wald t tests on 189 degrees of freedom; p-values and confidence limits adjusted by the single-step (Dunnett) method, 95% confidence limits.

# residuals of each plant correlated over time, continuous-time AR(1)
fitc <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, rform=b1 + b2 ~ 1 | Plant_ID, data=FabaHeights25,
              correlation=corCAR1(form=~ DAS | Plant_ID))
corpars(fitc)
#>      rho 
#> 0.953607 

# pod counts with a poisson distribution
gcTMB(Pods ~ DAS, data=FabaCounts23, family="poisson")
#> Call:
#> gcTMB(form = Pods ~ DAS, data = FabaCounts23, family = "poisson")
#> 
#> Model:  logistic, truncated at b4 = 0
#> Family: poisson, identity link for all parameters
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> b1:(Intercept)  b2:(Intercept)  b3:(Intercept)  
#>         16.361          71.947           1.569  

# no pods before a threshold b4, after which the count grows
